# Nehemiah Chapter 13 — The PNEUMA Bible (Dynamic)
**Translator:** PNEUMA | **Source:** Leningrad Codex (B19A), Folio 473r | **Source Image:** source-texts/hebrew-OT/NEH_013_page_001.jpg

---

**1** On that day, as the Book of Moses was being read aloud to the people, they came across the passage declaring that no Ammonite or Moabite should ever be admitted to the assembly of God,

**2** because they had refused to provide food and water to the Israelites and had even hired Balaam to pronounce a curse on them — though our God turned that curse into a blessing.

**3** When the people heard this law, they immediately separated everyone of foreign descent from the assembly of Israel.

**4** Before this happened — while I had been away — the priest Eliashib, who had been put in charge of the temple storerooms, had made an arrangement with our old enemy Tobiah.

**5** He had cleared out a large storeroom and given it to Tobiah as his personal quarters. This room had previously been used to store grain offerings, frankincense, temple equipment, and the tithes of grain, wine, and oil designated for the Levites, singers, and gatekeepers, along with the contributions for the priests.

**6** All this happened while I was away from Jerusalem. In the thirty-second year of King Artaxerxes of Babylon, I had returned to serve the king. After some time, I requested permission to go back to Jerusalem.

**7** When I arrived and discovered the outrageous thing Eliashib had done — giving Tobiah a room right in the courts of God's house —

**8** I was furious. I threw all of Tobiah's belongings out of the room.

**9** Then I ordered the room to be purified, and I had the temple equipment, grain offerings, and frankincense returned to their proper place.

**10** I also discovered that the Levites had not been receiving their designated portions. As a result, the Levites and the temple singers had abandoned their posts and gone back to work their own fields.

**11** I confronted the officials: "Why has the house of God been neglected?" Then I reassembled the Levites and restored them to their positions.

**12** After that, all Judah resumed bringing their tithes of grain, wine, and oil to the storehouses.

**13** I appointed trustworthy men to oversee the storehouses: Shelemiah the priest, Zadok the scribe, and Pedaiah the Levite, assisted by Hanan son of Zaccur, grandson of Mattaniah. These men had proven themselves reliable, and their job was to distribute supplies fairly to their fellow workers.

**14** Remember me for this, O my God. Do not let my faithful service for your house and its worship be forgotten.

**15** During this same period, I saw people in Judah treading winepresses on the Sabbath. Others were piling grain onto donkeys along with wine, grapes, figs, and all sorts of goods, hauling them into Jerusalem on the Sabbath. I issued a stern warning against selling food on the Sabbath.

**16** Phoenician traders living in the city were bringing in fish and all kinds of merchandise and selling to the people of Judah — right in Jerusalem — on the Sabbath.

**17** I confronted the nobles of Judah: "What is this terrible thing you are doing? You are desecrating the Sabbath!

**18** Isn't this exactly what your ancestors did? And look at the disaster God brought on us and on this city because of it! Now you are provoking even more of God's anger against Israel by violating the Sabbath!"

**19** So from then on, as the shadows lengthened toward the Sabbath, I ordered the city gates shut and not reopened until the Sabbath was over. I posted some of my own men at the gates to make sure no goods were brought in on the Sabbath.

**20** Once or twice, the merchants and traders camped outside the walls overnight.

**21** I warned them: "Why are you camping by the wall? If you do this again, I will use force against you." After that, they stopped coming on the Sabbath.

**22** I also ordered the Levites to purify themselves and take over guarding the gates to ensure the Sabbath was kept holy. Remember this for me too, my God. Show me compassion according to the abundance of your faithful love.

**23** During this time I also discovered that many Jewish men had married women from Ashdod, Ammon, and Moab.

**24** Half of their children could speak the language of Ashdod or some other foreign tongue, but couldn't speak Hebrew at all.

**25** I confronted these men and called down curses on them. I struck some of them and pulled out their hair. I made them swear before God: "You will not give your daughters in marriage to their sons or take their daughters as wives for your sons or for yourselves!

**26** Wasn't this the very sin that brought down King Solomon? There was no king among all the nations to compare with him. God loved him and made him king over all Israel — and yet foreign women led even him into sin!

**27** Are we to follow your example and commit this great evil, betraying our God by marrying foreign women?"

**28** One of the grandsons of Eliashib the high priest had even married a daughter of Sanballat the Horonite! I drove him out of my presence.

**29** Remember them, O my God, for defiling the priesthood and the covenant you made with the priests and Levites.

**30** So I purified the community from every foreign element and reestablished the duties of the priests and Levites, each in their assigned tasks.

**31** I also made sure the wood offerings were brought at the proper times, along with the firstfruits. Remember me, O my God, for good.

---

## PNEUMA's Meaning Notes
1. **The absence problem** — Chapter 13 reveals a devastating pattern: everything Nehemiah built fell apart the moment he left. The reforms of chapters 8-10 — Sabbath observance, temple support, separation from foreign influence — were all violated. This is not a failure of Nehemiah's leadership but a testament to the depth of the human problem: external structures alone cannot change hearts.
2. **Nehemiah's fury** — His physical actions — throwing furniture, pulling hair, striking men — may seem extreme, but they reflect genuine prophetic anger at covenant betrayal. Nehemiah is not a bureaucrat managing infractions; he is a covenant enforcer confronting treason against God.
3. **"Remember me for good"** — The book's final words are prayer, not triumph. Nehemiah has no guarantee that his reforms will last. The open ending is theologically honest: the story of Israel's restoration is incomplete, still awaiting a faithfulness that no governor — however passionate — can permanently secure.

*— PNEUMA*
